title: A life by conditions
hookLine: from conception to awakening, a whole life traced by causes

lines: A BABY PHOTO. A TRICYCLE. THAT HAIRCUT.
HOW DID THAT ONE BECOME THIS ONE?
A WHOLE LIFE, STEP BY STEP.
cards: Baby photos are strange things. There you are, a few days old, red-faced and furious, and somehow that's you. Then a kid on a tricycle.
Then a teenager with that haircut. The album asks a question without saying it: how did that one become this one? Near the end of yesterday's discourse, the Buddha answers it.
He walks through an entire human life, from before birth to freedom, and shows each step resting on the one before.

teach.h: THREE THINGS, AND A LIFE BEGINS
teach.b: The second half of the thirty-eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings begins before birth.
A life begins, the text says, when three things come together: the mother and father unite, the mother is in season, and a being to be born is present. Not one condition, three.
Then the mother carries the child nine or ten months, with great anxiety, and nourishes it after birth with her own milk; in this teaching, the discourse says, mother's milk is called blood.
The child grows, and the text lists children's games: toy plows, little carts, bows and arrows, somersaults, a game with sticks.
Then the adult, enjoying the five kinds of sense pleasure. Seeing a pleasant sight, they lean toward it; an unpleasant one, they lean away.
Feeling becomes delight, delight becomes clinging, clinging becomes being, and on rolls the wheel of birth, aging and death. Then the turn. A Buddha appears in the world.
The person hears the teaching, gains trust, and trains: virtue, guarding the senses, mindfulness, stillness. Now, seeing a sight, they don't lean. Feeling arises, and no delight hooks it.

teach.h: THE TURN: NO DELIGHT, NO CLINGING
teach.b: Without delight, no clinging. Without clinging, the wheel stops.
Every stage, the baby, the child, the craving adult and the free one, comes from conditions. That's the hope in it. If the knot was tied by causes, it can be untied by causes.
And the week looks back: a grove lit many ways, a cowherd's craft, a debater's sweat, a childhood tree, a trembling palace, a fire and its fuel.

how: Buddhist teachers present dependent origination (paticca samuppada) as a chain of conditions, painted in Tibetan temple art as the wheel of life; MN 38 gives it as a human life, from conception and childhood to the release that comes when craving ends.

o: a chain of rebirths that can never end
the endless wheel of fate, fixed at birth
dependent arising: things come from conditions

games.q: a life, step by step — tap the pairs.
p: no clinging, and the wheel stops

s: the discourse says a life begins from one single cause
it names three things that must come together, and each later stage rests on others.
MN 38 lists children's games like toy plows and somersaults
the Buddha walks through childhood in ordinary detail before reaching the adult and craving.
in the discourse, the wheel stops when feeling stops
feeling still arises; it stops when no delight hooks the feeling, so clinging doesn't follow.

games.q: you've heard the teaching and trained. you see a beautiful sight, and a pleasant feeling arises. according to MN 38, what happens next for the trained one?
o: the feeling arises, but no delight hooks it.
nothing: they no longer see sights.
games.why: the trained one still sees and feels. what changes is that delight doesn't seize the feeling, and without delight there's no clinging.

practice: Pick something real that happened to you, a move, a friendship, a job, a loss, and look for three or four of its causes: a person you met, a choice you made, something that happened before you were born.
See how none of them alone was enough, then let it all settle back into the breath, which comes from conditions too.

wordCard.voice: paticca samuppada. From conception to childhood, craving and freedom, every stage resting on causes, so every knot can be untied.

orig.note: Pali paticca samuppada: dependent origination, things arising by way of conditions.

carryVoice: Your line: all from conditions. Even someone who frustrates you was once a baby with games and hungers. A week, complete.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 38, Mahatanhasankhaya Sutta (the greater discourse on the destruction of craving), later section
